title: Financial Accounting I
source_note: Grounded in standard introductory financial accounting curriculum (accounting concepts, double-entry, ledgers, trial balance, final accounts of sole traders, depreciation, bad debts, bank reconciliation, control accounts, inventory valuation, correction of errors) as taught in NUC-aligned Nigerian university accounting programmes.

questions.question: The accounting concept which assumes that a business will continue operating for the foreseeable future, rather than being liquidated, is known as the:
options: Going concern concept
Prudence concept
Money measurement concept
Realisation concept
questions.correct_answer: Going concern concept
questions.explanation: The going concern concept assumes the business will continue in operation long enough to carry out its existing commitments, which justifies valuing assets at cost rather than break-up value.

questions.question: Under the accrual (matching) concept, revenue and costs are recognised:
options: As they are earned or incurred, not as cash is received or paid
Only when cash is received or paid
Only at the end of the accounting year
Only when a formal invoice is issued
questions.correct_answer: As they are earned or incurred, not as cash is received or paid
questions.explanation: The accrual concept requires that income and expenses be matched to the period in which they are earned or incurred regardless of the timing of cash movement.

questions.question: The prudence (conservatism) concept requires that:
options: Revenue is recognised only when reasonably certain, but losses are provided for as soon as anticipated
Profits and losses are both recognised only when cash changes hands
All anticipated profits and losses are ignored until realised
Assets are always shown at their highest possible value
questions.correct_answer: Revenue is recognised only when reasonably certain, but losses are provided for as soon as anticipated
questions.explanation: Prudence means anticipating no profit but providing for all possible losses, so financial statements are not overstated.

questions.question: The consistency concept in accounting means that:
options: The same accounting methods should be applied from one period to the next unless there is good reason to change
All businesses in an industry must use identical accounting policies
Figures must remain unchanged once published
Only cash-based methods should be used consistently
questions.correct_answer: The same accounting methods should be applied from one period to the next unless there is good reason to change
questions.explanation: Consistency ensures that financial statements are comparable across periods by applying the same accounting treatment year after year.

questions.question: The business entity concept requires that:
options: The financial affairs of the business are kept separate from the personal affairs of the owner
The business must be a registered legal entity such as a limited company
Only large businesses need to keep accounting records
Owners' personal assets are included in the business balance sheet
questions.correct_answer: The financial affairs of the business are kept separate from the personal affairs of the owner
questions.explanation: Under the business entity concept, the business is treated as a unit separate from its owner(s) for accounting purposes, even where it has no separate legal identity, as in a sole proprietorship.

questions.question: Under the historical cost concept, assets are normally recorded in the accounts at:
options: Their original purchase cost
Their current market value
Their estimated replacement cost
Their net realisable value
questions.correct_answer: Their original purchase cost
questions.explanation: The historical cost concept states that assets are recorded at the amount actually paid to acquire them, providing an objective and verifiable basis for accounting.

questions.question: Under the double-entry rule, an increase in an asset account is recorded as a:
options: Debit
Credit
Either debit or credit depending on the asset
Neither, assets are not recorded in ledger accounts
questions.correct_answer: Debit
questions.explanation: Assets have debit balances, so an increase in an asset is recorded on the debit side of the relevant ledger account.

questions.question: Under the double-entry rule, an increase in a liability account is recorded as a:
options: Credit
Debit
Neither debit nor credit
A contra entry only
questions.correct_answer: Credit
questions.explanation: Liabilities carry credit balances, so an increase in a liability is recorded on the credit side of the account.

questions.question: The main purpose of preparing a trial balance is to:
options: Check the arithmetical accuracy of the double-entry postings
Show the profit or loss for the period
Show the financial position of the business
Replace the need for a balance sheet
questions.correct_answer: Check the arithmetical accuracy of the double-entry postings
questions.explanation: A trial balance lists all ledger balances to confirm that total debits equal total credits, revealing certain types of arithmetical error.

questions.question: Which of the following errors will NOT be revealed by a trial balance?
options: Error of complete omission, where a transaction is left out of the books entirely
A debit entry posted without a corresponding credit entry
A trial balance addition error
Posting only one side of a transaction
questions.correct_answer: Error of complete omission, where a transaction is left out of the books entirely
questions.explanation: An error of complete omission affects neither the debit nor the credit side, so the trial balance still balances even though a transaction is missing.

questions.question: An error of principle occurs when:
options: A transaction is recorded in the wrong class of account, e.g. capital expenditure treated as revenue expenditure
Figures are transposed, e.g. 540 entered as 450
A transaction is completely omitted from the books
Two errors cancel each other out
questions.correct_answer: A transaction is recorded in the wrong class of account, e.g. capital expenditure treated as revenue expenditure
questions.explanation: An error of principle happens when the correct amount is entered but in the wrong type of account, violating an accounting principle, such as treating a capital item as an expense.

questions.question: A compensating error occurs when:
options: Two or more errors of equal and opposite amounts cancel each other out, so the trial balance still balances
A transaction is posted to the wrong personal account
An asset is undervalued in the balance sheet
A ledger account is never opened
questions.correct_answer: Two or more errors of equal and opposite amounts cancel each other out, so the trial balance still balances
questions.explanation: Compensating errors offset one another in value, so although two mistakes exist, the trial balance totals still agree.

questions.question: A suspense account is opened in the ledger primarily to:
options: Temporarily hold the difference when a trial balance fails to balance, pending investigation
Record all cash transactions of the business
Replace the need for a bank account
Record depreciation on non-current assets
questions.correct_answer: Temporarily hold the difference when a trial balance fails to balance, pending investigation
questions.explanation: A suspense account is a temporary account used to balance the books when errors causing an imbalance have not yet been located and corrected.

questions.question: A non-current asset is purchased for ₦100,000 with an estimated residual value of ₦10,000 and a useful life of 5 years. Using the straight-line method, the annual depreciation charge is:
questions.explanation: Straight-line depreciation = (Cost - Residual value) / Useful life = (100,000 - 10,000) / 5 = ₦18,000 per year.

questions.question: An asset costing ₦50,000 is depreciated at 20% per annum using the reducing balance method. The depreciation charge for the second year is:
questions.explanation: Year 1 depreciation = 50,000 x 20% = 10,000, giving a net book value of 40,000. Year 2 depreciation = 40,000 x 20% = ₦8,000.

questions.question: The main reason non-current assets are depreciated in the accounts is to:
options: Spread the cost of the asset over its useful life and match it against the revenue it helps generate
Set aside cash to replace the asset when it wears out
Reduce the amount of tax payable
Show the asset at its current market value
questions.correct_answer: Spread the cost of the asset over its useful life and match it against the revenue it helps generate
questions.explanation: Depreciation applies the matching/accrual concept by allocating an asset's cost as an expense over the periods that benefit from its use; it is not a cash-setting-aside mechanism.

questions.question: The difference between 'bad debts' and 'provision for doubtful debts' is that:
options: Bad debts are debts already confirmed irrecoverable and written off, while a provision is an estimate for debts that may become uncollectible
Bad debts relate to non-current assets while provisions relate to current assets
Provision for doubtful debts is written off directly to the debtor's account
There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable
questions.correct_answer: Bad debts are debts already confirmed irrecoverable and written off, while a provision is an estimate for debts that may become uncollectible
questions.explanation: A bad debt is a specific debt known to be irrecoverable, whereas a provision for doubtful debts is a general estimate, in line with the prudence concept, for debts that might not be collected.

questions.question: Trade debtors at the year end are ₦20,000. The business wishes to maintain a provision for doubtful debts of 5%. The provision required is:
questions.explanation: Provision required = 5% x ₦20,000 = ₦1,000.

questions.question: In a bank reconciliation statement, an unpresented cheque (one written by the business but not yet cleared by the bank) is treated by:
options: Deducting it from the bank statement balance to arrive at the cash book balance
Adding it to the cash book balance
Deducting it from the cash book balance
Ignoring it entirely as it has no effect
questions.correct_answer: Deducting it from the bank statement balance to arrive at the cash book balance
questions.explanation: An unpresented cheque has already reduced the cash book balance but has not yet been deducted by the bank, so it must be subtracted from the bank statement balance during reconciliation.

questions.question: A cheque lodged by the business but not yet credited by the bank (uncredited lodgement) is treated in the bank reconciliation statement by:
options: Adding it to the bank statement balance
Deducting it from the bank statement balance
Adding it to the cash book balance
Deducting it from the cash book balance
questions.correct_answer: Adding it to the bank statement balance
questions.explanation: An uncredited lodgement has already been recorded as a receipt in the cash book but the bank has not yet processed it, so it is added to the bank statement balance to reconcile the two figures.

questions.question: The primary purpose of a sales ledger (debtors) control account is to:
options: Provide a check on the accuracy of the individual debtors' accounts in the sales ledger
Record cash purchases of inventory
Calculate the depreciation on trade receivables
Replace the need to keep individual customer accounts
questions.correct_answer: Provide a check on the accuracy of the individual debtors' accounts in the sales ledger
questions.explanation: A control account summarises all entries affecting debtors as a whole, and its balance should agree with the total of the individual debtor balances, helping to detect errors.

questions.question: Opening debtors were ₦5,000. During the period, credit sales were ₦40,000, cash received from debtors was ₦38,000, discount allowed was ₦500, and returns inward were ₦300. The closing balance on the sales ledger control account is:
questions.explanation: Closing debtors = Opening debtors + Credit sales - Cash received - Discount allowed - Returns inward = 5,000 + 40,000 - 38,000 - 500 - 300 = ₦6,200.

questions.question: A business had purchases during the year of 100 units at ₦10 each, followed by 150 units at ₦12 each. It later sold 120 units. Using the FIFO (first-in, first-out) method, the value of closing inventory is:
questions.explanation: Under FIFO, the 120 units sold are assumed to be the first 100 units at ₦10 plus 20 units at ₦12, leaving 130 units at ₦12 each in closing inventory: 130 x 12 = ₦1,560.

questions.question: If closing inventory is overstated at the end of an accounting period, the effect on that period's reported net profit is that it will be:
options: Overstated
Understated
Unaffected
Understated only if the business uses FIFO
questions.correct_answer: Overstated
questions.explanation: Closing inventory is deducted in arriving at cost of goods sold; overstating it understates cost of sales, which in turn overstates gross and net profit.

questions.question: At the year end, rent of ₦6,000 has been incurred for the period but not yet paid. In the final accounts, this should be treated as a(n):
options: Accrued expense, added to the rent expense in the profit and loss account and shown as a current liability
Prepaid expense, deducted from the rent expense and shown as a current asset
Item ignored until it is actually paid
Reduction in capital only
questions.correct_answer: Accrued expense, added to the rent expense in the profit and loss account and shown as a current liability
questions.explanation: Under the accrual concept, expenses incurred but not yet paid must be added to the expense for the period and recognised as a current liability (accrued expense) in the balance sheet.

questions.question: Insurance of ₦12,000 was paid during the year, of which ₦2,000 relates to the following accounting period. In the final accounts, the ₦2,000 should be:
options: Deducted from the insurance expense and shown as a prepayment (current asset)
Added to the insurance expense and shown as a current liability
Treated as a bad debt
Ignored since it was already paid in cash
questions.correct_answer: Deducted from the insurance expense and shown as a prepayment (current asset)
questions.explanation: The ₦2,000 relates to a future period, so it is not an expense of the current period; it is removed from the expense charge and carried forward as a prepaid expense (current asset).

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of capital expenditure, as opposed to revenue expenditure?
options: Cost of installing a new delivery van, including delivery and set-up costs
Cost of fuel for the delivery van
Cost of repairing a broken window in the office
Wages paid to shop assistants
questions.correct_answer: Cost of installing a new delivery van, including delivery and set-up costs
questions.explanation: Capital expenditure is incurred to acquire or improve a non-current asset and provides benefit over more than one accounting period, such as the purchase and installation cost of a van; running costs like fuel and repairs are revenue expenditure.

questions.question: A business has sales of ₦200,000, opening inventory of ₦20,000, purchases of ₦150,000, and closing inventory of ₦30,000. The gross profit for the period is:
questions.explanation: Cost of goods sold = Opening inventory + Purchases - Closing inventory = 20,000 + 150,000 - 30,000 = 140,000. Gross profit = Sales - COGS = 200,000 - 140,000 = ₦60,000.

questions.question: Using the gross profit of ₦60,000 calculated for a business, if total operating expenses for the period are ₦25,000, the net profit is:
questions.explanation: Net profit = Gross profit - Operating expenses = 60,000 - 25,000 = ₦35,000.

questions.question: A business has current assets of ₦80,000 and current liabilities of ₦50,000. Its working capital is:
questions.explanation: Working capital = Current assets - Current liabilities = 80,000 - 50,000 = ₦30,000.

questions.question: A sole trader who does not keep proper double-entry records has total assets of ₦120,000 and total liabilities of ₦40,000 at the start of the year. Using the statement of affairs method, the opening capital is:
questions.explanation: Under the accounting equation, Capital = Assets - Liabilities = 120,000 - 40,000 = ₦80,000, which is the basis of the statement of affairs used with incomplete records.

questions.question: In a partnership's profit and loss appropriation account, interest on partners' capital is:
options: An appropriation of profit shared among partners, not a charge against profit before arriving at net profit
Deducted in the trading account before gross profit is calculated
Treated in the same way as bank loan interest
Only allowed if the partnership deed is silent on the matter
questions.correct_answer: An appropriation of profit shared among partners, not a charge against profit before arriving at net profit
questions.explanation: Interest on capital, salaries to partners, and profit shares are all appropriations made after net profit has been determined, distinguishing them from expenses charged in arriving at net profit.

questions.question: IFRS, the set of accounting standards increasingly adopted in Nigeria, stands for:
options: International Financial Reporting Standards
Internal Financial Regulation System
International Fiscal Reporting Structure
Institute of Financial Reporting Standards
questions.correct_answer: International Financial Reporting Standards
questions.explanation: IFRS refers to International Financial Reporting Standards, issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) and adopted for financial reporting in Nigeria.

questions.question: The materiality concept in accounting means that:
options: Only items significant enough to influence the decisions of users of the financial statements need be treated strictly according to accounting principles
Every transaction, however small, must be disclosed in a separate note
Only material (physical) assets are recorded in the accounts
Financial statements must be audited before publication
questions.correct_answer: Only items significant enough to influence the decisions of users of the financial statements need be treated strictly according to accounting principles
questions.explanation: Materiality allows immaterial items to be treated in the most convenient way, since strict accounting treatment is reserved for items large or significant enough to affect users' decisions.

questions.question: In a balance sheet, which of the following would be classified as a current asset?
options: Inventory (stock)
Motor vehicles
Goodwill
Long-term investment property
questions.correct_answer: Inventory (stock)
questions.explanation: Inventory is expected to be sold or converted to cash within the normal operating cycle (usually one year), making it a current asset, unlike motor vehicles and goodwill which are non-current.

questions.question: Which financial statement primarily shows the financial position of a business as at a specific date?
options: The balance sheet (statement of financial position)
The trading and profit and loss account
The cash flow statement
The trial balance
questions.correct_answer: The balance sheet (statement of financial position)
questions.explanation: The balance sheet reports assets, liabilities and capital as at a particular point in time, while the trading and profit and loss account covers performance over a period.
